newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Central bank goes public about gold selldown.
newsitem.headline: Central bank goes public about gold selldown.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia took the rare step on Thursday of publicly responding to media reports of a potential conflict of interest in its board's decision to sell down the nation's gold reserves.
The RBA announced two weeks ago that it had sold 167 tonnes of gold, or two-thirds of its reserves -- news that helped push the precious metal to 12-year lows on world markets.

The decision was made by the RBA board, whose members included Hugh Morgan, managing director of miner WMC Ltd -- a company that has forward sold more than three million ounces of gold to hedge against a weak gold price.
On Thursday morning, Prime Minister John Howard said he would inquire into Morgan's involvement.
The industry blames the RBA's staged sale, announced on July 4 after its completion, for fuelling the metal's price fall -- making many of Australia's high-cost mines no longer commercial.
"I don't know what happened at the Reserve Bank board meeting," Howard said in a radio interview.
"I will be making some inquiries to inform myself."
Morgan responded with a statement saying that he had never used information gained as a board member to benefit his company or passed such information on to any company executive.
He also said he had never used privileged information to encourage or discourage WMC executives to do anything they were not already planning to do.

"I have followed this principle because it is ethically correct and because it conforms with the legal and secrecy provisions I agreed to when I joined the Reserve Bank Board," Morgan said in a statement.

"I believe that I have correctly taken the view that to excuse myself from normal duties within the company could have alerted people both inside and outside the company of a forthcoming unusual transaction."
The Reserve Bank is normally very secretive about its activities and does not comment on press reports but RBA governor Ian Macfarlane issued a statement backing Morgan.

"It is inevitable that potential conflicts will arise from time to time for members of a Board which has the responsibility to make decisions affecting the economy as a whole, as well as particular sectors of the economy," Macfarlane said.

"This is a consequence of the longstanding arrangements in Australia which seek to bring a range of commercial and other private sector expertise and knowledge to bear on the central bank's policy-making."
Macfarlane dismissed suggestions that Morgan should not have taken part in the board's discussions on the subject.

In appointing board members, he added, the bank selected people judged to have high ethical standards able to dissociate their personal and business interests from the national interests with which the RBA was concerned.
"On the basis of my discussions with Mr Morgan, and the statement he issued today, I am satisfied that Mr Morgan has fulfilled his obligation as a Board member," Macfarlane concluded.
The RBA has been hit by a storm of criticism over its gold sales. Australian miners have complained that many of their operations had been made uneconomic by the fall in the price of bullion.

Leading miners said the RBA should have been more sensitive to the needs of Australia's second most valuable export industry instead of sending a signal to world markets that gold was no longer worth holding.

Announcing the sales, the RBA argued that it made no sense for a gold-rich country like Australia to hold large official gold reserves. The estimated US$1.8 billion raised by the sales had been transferred into foreign currency assets such as bonds.
A WMC spokesman said late on Wednesday that the miner had set its gold heding strategy in May 1996 -- before Morgan had even joined the board.
